newsitem.title: FRANCE: French strikes could hit international air travel.
newsitem.headline: French strikes could hit international air travel.

text.p: France faces a barrage of strikes likely to be felt beyond its borders on Thursday, as action by air traffic controllers threatens international air travel.

Serious disruptions are predicted on domestic flights, expected to number no more than about 550, air travel industry specialists said. Only some 300 will be to or from Paris' Orly and Roissy airports intead of the usual 1,750 there daily.

But the great unknown is how the air traffic controllers will handle an estimated 5,000 flights over France between north and southern European destinations and between other European countries and North America, the sources said.
Some foreign companies have already started to plan flights with itineraries avoiding French air space altogether, the sources said.
The nationwide strikes kicked off late on Wednesday with stoppages by railwayworkers. They were expected to continue throughout Thursday in schools, hospitals, trains and other services.
The rail strike was expected to halt between 30 and 60 percent of trains although the London-Paris Eurostar train under the English Channel was due to provide full service.

The 24-hour strike is spearheaded by civil servants who are fighting government plans to trim their numbers by nearly 6,000 next year as part of a drive to get French finances in order to qualify for monetary union and a single European currency. Air traffic controllers are civil servants.
The seven main civil service unions have organised a march in central Paris on Thursday from the Place de la Republique.
The strikes are the first big wave of labour unrest since crippling strikes in late 1995.

Government offices and agencies face disruption or closure for the day and workers at the state-owned gas and electricity companies will also stop work, but power cuts are not expected. Postal workers will also join the action.
Teachers will bear the brunt of the austerity drive, with a loss of 2,300 permanent jobs and the layoff of some 15,000 short-term contract staff.

The other motive for the strike is frustration over record 12.6 percent unemployment, with more than three million jobless despite President Jacques Chirac's May 1995 election pledge to make employment his top priority.
A poll due to appear in Thursday's Parisien daily shows 64 percent of those polled support or sympathise with the strike.
Doctors will also protest for 24 hours on Thursday over government health care reforms.
Some disruption is also expected on Paris buses, the Metro underground rail service and the suburban RER commuter lines.
